claims.text: The starting material is as-received, unmodified Q235 steel with its native microstructure and composition.
Q235 steel develops a transient intermediate Fe-oxide phase during high-temperature Na2SO4 exposure.
The transient Fe-oxide phase acts as a kinetic barrier to corrosive species.
The transient phase retards diffusion of oxygen through the developing scale.
The transient phase retards transport of Na+ and sulfate-derived aggressive species.
Persistence of the transient phase enables gradual formation of a coherent, continuous, and adherent protective oxide scale.
Absence or rapid conversion of the transient phase produces scale defects that permit accelerated oxidation and degradation.
Q235 specimens will be heated from room temperature to 900 °C under Na2SO4-deposited and salt-free conditions.
Tests will include holds at 700 °C and 900 °C to resolve transient and mature oxide phases.
In-situ synchrotron XRD and TGA will track oxide-phase evolution and oxidation mass change, respectively.
Specimens exhibiting a clearly detected and persistent transient phase will have lower mass gain than specimens in which that phase is absent or short-lived.
Specimens exhibiting the transient phase will retain more hardness after exposure.
Specimens exhibiting the transient phase will develop a more continuous and adherent oxide scale.
Salt-free Q235 will oxidize more gradually than salt-exposed Q235.
Na2SO4 interference accelerates degradation relative to salt-free oxidation.
The proposed transient-phase mechanism applies specifically to salt exposure at 700–900 °C.
At room temperature or under salt-free conditions, different oxidation pathways dominate and the transient-phase mechanism is less relevant.
Variation in the initial Q235 microstructure may affect transient-phase evolution and corrosion protection.
Failure to observe improved mass gain, hardness retention, or scale morphology in specimens with a clear transient-phase signature would falsify the proposed correlation.
